clean_source_blocks.text: International rescue teams and humanitarian aid are pouring into Venezuela as authorities race to find survivors trapped beneath collapsed buildings after two powerful earthquakes devastated the country. The death toll from devastating earthquakes in Venezuela has climbed to 920, with at least 3,360 people injured, as emergency crews continue large-scale search and rescue operations across heavily damaged regions of the country. Authorities said rescue teams are still working through collapsed buildings and unstable debris fields, where hundreds of people are believed to remain trapped. Officials warned that the number of casualties could rise further as access to some of the worst-hit areas remains limited due to damaged roads and disrupted communications. The earthquakes, which struck earlier this week, caused widespread destruction across multiple states, flattening residential neighborhoods, damaging critical infrastructure and leaving entire communities isolated. 'They are all I have': Mother searches for missing daughters More than 900 people have been killed and 3,360 others injured in the Venezuela earthquakes, according to the government, as rescuers keep searching for survivors and families wait desperately for news. The injured are being treated in makeshift medical facilities after dozens of buildings in the country's north were destroyed by the two quakes, including in the capital Caracas. A senior government official said hundreds of international rescue workers have arrived in the country, with more on the way. Two powerful earthquakes rocked Venezuela within seconds of each other on Wednesday. The second quake was one of the strongest tremors to hit the country in a century, at a magnitude of 7.5. Devastating images from the Venezuelan earthquake 'I thought I was going to die' - Venezuelans describe earthquake panic

Venezuela earthquakes in maps and graphics - where they hit and how severe they could be La Guaira, a region north of the capital, has been hit the hardest, officials said. The state is also home to one of the country's two main ports and to Simón Bolívar International Airport in Maiquetía - the country's main airport. Many people are missing, and it is likely the death toll will rise as rescue efforts continue. In La Guaira, Natacha Diaz told the BBC that her two daughters - aged 22 and 23 - were trapped under the rubble of a collapsed shopping centre, where they worked as manicurists. "They were with their friends," she said. "I just want them to be found. I have faith and hope that they are there."
Hundreds are still feared trapped under the rubble, as families desperate for news.

The injured are being treated in makeshift medical facilities after dozens of buildings in the country's north were destroyed by the two quakes, including in the capital Caracas.

A senior government official said hundreds of international rescue workers have arrived in the country, with more on the way.

Two powerful earthquakes rocked Venezuela within seconds of each other on Wednesday. The second quake was one of the strongest tremors to hit the country in a century, at a magnitude of 7.5.

La Guaira, a region north of the capital, has been hit the hardest, officials said. The state is also home to one of the country's two main ports and to Simón Bolívar International Airport in Maiquetía - the country's main airport.

Many people are missing, and it is likely the death toll will rise as rescue efforts continue.

In La Guaira, Natacha Diaz told the BBC that her two daughters - aged 22 and 23 - were trapped under the rubble of a collapsed shopping centre, where they worked as manicurists.

"They were with their friends," she said. "I just want them to be found. I have faith and hope that they are there."

"I just want them back with me. They are all I have, please."

National assembly head Jorge Rodriguez said in a state TV broadcast on Friday that the death toll had reached 920, with at least 172 people still believed to be trapped.

[Lähde: BBC]
The number of people killed in two Venezuelan earthquakes has risen to at least 920, with 3,360 injured, according to officials

In Caracas, overwhelmed rescuers are "pulling people out with their bare hands", a student tells the BBC

Natacha Diaz, a mother of two missing women, says her daughters "are all I have" - watch what else she says

Others are also trying to reach their relatives - Marianella tells BBC News Mundo "my heart tells me my brother is alive"

International rescue teams, bringing along sniffer dogs, have joined the search for survivors

The quakes, with magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5, hit a minute apart on Wednesday night, and the second was the strongest to hit Venezuela since 1900 - here's what else we know

You can also follow the latest updates on BBC News Mundo

Photographs taken in the hours since the tremors struck show residents gathered along the streets of Venezuela's capital, after their homes shook and the power went out.

Some hug their siblings and pets, while rescuers sift through debris for those trapped.

Authorities fear high casualties, but the full extent of damage is still unknown.

BBC News Mundo contributor Nicole Kolster said earlier that people could be heard calling for help from under the rubble of a collapsed building.

“‘Ask for help. We’re here,’ is what you can hear,” she said.

After the quake, others were "still outside waiting for safety in case there’s an aftershock,” Kolster added.

“The recommendation is not to go back up into the building,” she explained.

Maria Elise, a local from the Caracas suburb of Palos Grandes, described how her apartment "has some cracked walls. There are fallen utility poles, we have no electricity, no signal."

Footage from the ground, captured by BBC reporter Vanessa Silva, shows rescuers searching for survivors under the debris of a collapsed multi-storey building in the north Caracas suburb of San Bernardino.

Unconfirmed reports suggest that at least one person has died in the neighbourhood.

Twin earthquakes have caused multiple buildings to collapse in the Venezuelan capital, and authorities fear there could be high casualties and extensive damage across the city.

Maiquetía airport, Venezuela's main international airport, has been closed due to "serious damage" from the earthquake, Rodríguez says.

payload.title: Venezuelan maanjäristyksissä kuollut 920 ihmistä
payload.summary: Venezuelassa kahden voimakkaan maanjäristyksen uhriluku on noussut 920:een. Pelastustyöt jatkuvat, ja satojen ihmisten pelätään olevan yhä raunioissa.
payload.content:
Venezuelassa kahden voimakkaan maanjäristyksen uhriluku on noussut 920:een, ja ainakin 3 360 ihmistä on loukkaantunut viranomaisten mukaan. Kansainvälisiä pelastustyöntekijöitä ja humanitaarista apua on saapunut maahan, kun etsintäryhmät yrittävät löytää eloonjääneitä sortuneiden rakennusten alta ja perheet odottavat tietoja kadonneista omaisistaan.

## Pelastustyöt jatkuvat vaikeissa oloissa

Maanjäristykset iskivät keskiviikkona vain sekuntien välein. Jälkimmäisen järistyksen voimakkuudeksi on kerrottu 7,5, ja sitä on kuvattu yhdeksi Venezuelan voimakkaimmista järistyksistä vuosisataan.

Viranomaisten mukaan pelastajat työskentelevät sortuneissa rakennuksissa ja epävakailla raunioalueilla, joissa satojen ihmisten uskotaan olevan yhä jumissa. Uhriluvun pelätään nousevan, sillä pääsy osaan pahimmin vaurioituneista alueista on vaikeaa vaurioituneiden teiden ja häiriintyneiden viestiyhteyksien vuoksi.

Järistykset ovat aiheuttaneet laajaa tuhoa useissa osavaltioissa. Asuinalueita on tuhoutunut, keskeistä infrastruktuuria on vaurioitunut ja kokonaisia yhteisöjä on jäänyt eristyksiin. Loukkaantuneita hoidetaan tilapäisissä hoitopaikoissa sen jälkeen, kun kymmeniä rakennuksia maan pohjoisosissa, myös pääkaupunki Caracasissa, tuhoutui.

## Kansainvälistä apua saapuu

Viranomaislähteen mukaan maahan on jo saapunut satoja kansainvälisiä pelastustyöntekijöitä, ja lisää on matkalla. Avun tarve on suuri, koska etsinnät jatkuvat laajoilla vaurioalueilla samaan aikaan, kun sairaanhoito joutuu hoitamaan tuhansia loukkaantuneita poikkeusoloissa.

## La Guaira kärsi pahimmin

Viranomaisten mukaan pahimmin on kärsinyt pääkaupunki Caracasin pohjoispuolella sijaitseva La Guairan alue. Se on myös tärkeä liikenteen solmukohta, sillä alueella sijaitsevat yksi maan kahdesta pääsatamasta sekä Maiquetían Simón Bolívarin kansainvälinen lentoasema.

Monet perheet odottavat yhä tietoja kadonneista omaisistaan. La Guairassa Natacha Diaz kertoi etsivänsä kahta tytärtään, 22- ja 23-vuotiaita naisia, joiden kerrottiin jääneen sortuneen ostoskeskuksen raunioihin. Tyttäret työskentelivät siellä manikyristeinä.

Diazin mukaan hänen tyttärensä olivat ystäviensä kanssa, kun rakennus sortui. Hän sanoi haluavansa vain, että heidät löydetään, ja kertoi pitävänsä yhä kiinni uskosta ja toivosta heidän löytymisestään.
summary_bullets: Viranomaisten mukaan Venezuelan maanjäristyksissä on kuollut 920 ihmistä ja loukkaantunut ainakin 3 360.
Kansainvälisiä pelastustyöntekijöitä on saapunut maahan, ja lisää on tulossa.
Satojen ihmisten pelätään olevan yhä raunioissa, ja uhriluvun arvioidaan voivan nousta.

Officials warned that the number of casualties could rise further as access to some of the worst-hit areas remains limited due to damaged roads and disrupted communications. The earthquakes, which struck earlier this week, caused widespread destruction across multiple states, flattening residential neighborhoods, damaging critical infrastructure and leaving entire communities isolated. 'They are all I have': Mother searches for missing daughters More than 900 people have been killed and 3,360 others injured in the Venezuela earthquakes, according to the government, as rescuers keep searching for survivors and families wait desperately for news. The injured are being treated in makeshift medical facilities after dozens of buildings in the country's north were destroyed by the two quakes, including in the capital Caracas. A senior government official said hundreds of international rescue workers have arrived in the country, with more on the way. Two powerful earthquakes rocked Venezuela within seconds of each other on Wednesday. The second quake was one of the strongest tremors to hit the country in a century, at a magnitude of 7.5.
